## Purpose

This procedure describes field methods for monitoring wetland
hydrology, including measurement of water table depth, surface
inundation extent, and hydroperiod documentation. Hydrology is the
primary driver of wetland ecosystem structure and function: it controls
soil saturation, redox chemistry, plant community composition, and
jurisdictional wetland status under the Clean Water Act
[@mitsch2015; @usace1987].

Wetland hydrology monitoring supports baseline characterization,
impact assessment, restoration monitoring, and regulatory compliance
(e.g., Army Corps of Engineers wetland delineation criteria).


## Scope

- **Applies to:** Freshwater wetlands (marshes, swamps, riparian
  wetlands, vernal pools, constructed wetlands) at EA Program field
  sites. Methods include manual water-level measurements in
  monitoring wells and piezometers, crest gauges, staff gauges, and
  automated water level loggers.
- **Does not apply to:** Tidal wetland hydrology (requires tide-
  corrected methods); stream stage-discharge relationships (see
  [SOP-F301](SOP-F301-stream-discharge-measurement.qmd)); groundwater
  monitoring in non-wetland wells (see
  [SOP-F303](SOP-F303-groundwater-sampling.qmd))
- **Location:** All EA Program wetland field sites


## Responsibilities

| Role              | Responsibility                              |
|:------------------|:--------------------------------------------|
| PI / Field Lead   | Approve monitoring design, coordinate permits |
| Trained Personnel | Install equipment, collect data per this SOP |
| New Students      | Complete training before independent use    |


## Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **Physical:** Wetland substrates are unstable; risk of sinking in
  soft muck, tripping on submerged debris, or falling. Standing water
  may conceal holes and channels.
- **Biological:** Mosquitoes (disease vectors), ticks, venomous
  snakes, poison oak/ivy, and waterborne pathogens. Avoid direct
  skin contact with standing water.
- **Environmental:** Heat stress in summer; hypothermia in winter.
  Wetlands offer little shade.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Rubber boots or chest waders
- [ ] Nitrile gloves
- [ ] Long sleeves and pants (tick and mosquito protection)
- [ ] Insect repellent (DEET or picaridin)
- [ ] Sun protection (hat, sunscreen)
- [ ] Personal flotation device (if water depth exceeds knee level)

### Emergency Procedures

Work in pairs. If a team member becomes stuck in soft substrate,
distribute weight on a board or backpack and pull laterally rather
than vertically. Refer to
[SOP-F001 Field Safety](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd).


## Equipment and Materials

### Manual Measurement

| Item                                  | Notes                          |
|:--------------------------------------|:-------------------------------|
| Water level indicator (electric tape, e-line) | For measuring depth to water in wells and piezometers |
| Staff gauge (graduated, metric)       | For measuring surface water stage |
| Crest gauge                           | Records peak water level between visits |
| Meter stick or folding rule           | Backup; for shallow inundation depth |
| Field notebook and data sheets        | Waterproof (Rite in the Rain)  |
| GPS unit                              | Per [SOP-F006](SOP-F006-gps-site-navigation.qmd) |
| Camera                                | For photo-documenting site conditions |

### Automated Monitoring

| Item                                  | Notes                          |
|:--------------------------------------|:-------------------------------|
| Pressure transducer water level logger (e.g., HOBO U20L, Solinst Levelogger, In-Situ Level TROLL) | Deployed in wells or stilling wells |
| Barometric pressure logger            | Required for compensating non-vented transducers; install above the high water line at or near the site |
| PVC monitoring wells (2 in or 4 in diameter, slotted screen) | Installed per Section 6.1 |
| Well caps and locks                   | To prevent tampering and wildlife entry |
| Well keys or locks                    | For secured installations      |
| Laptop or shuttle for data download   | With manufacturer software     |


## Procedure

### Monitoring Well Installation

::: {.callout-note}
Well installation may require permits (e.g., well permits, Section 404
permits for work in wetlands). Confirm requirements with the PI before
installation.
:::

1. Select well locations based on the study design (e.g., transect
   from upland to wetland center, paired wells at different depths)
2. Auger a borehole to the target depth (typically 1--2 m for shallow
   water table monitoring)
3. Install a 2-inch or 4-inch PVC well with a slotted screen in the
   saturated zone and a solid riser above the ground surface
4. Backfill the annular space around the screen with clean silica sand;
   seal the upper portion with bentonite to prevent surface water
   infiltration along the well casing
5. Install a protective well cap; record the top-of-casing (TOC)
   elevation relative to a local benchmark using a survey level
6. Develop the well by surging and bailing to remove drilling mud and
   fine sediment. Allow the well to equilibrate for at least 24 hours
   before the first measurement.
7. Record the well construction details (total depth, screen interval,
   stick-up height, TOC elevation, GPS coordinates) on the well
   installation log

### Manual Water Level Measurement

1. Remove the well cap. If the well is locked, note the time and
   condition of the lock.
2. Lower the water level indicator (e-line) slowly into the well. When
   the probe contacts the water surface, the indicator will sound or
   light up.
3. Read the depth to water from the top of casing (TOC) to the nearest
   0.01 ft or 0.5 cm. Record this value.
4. Calculate the water table elevation:

   $$
   \text{WTE} = \text{TOC elevation} - \text{depth to water}
   $$

5. If the water table is above the ground surface (artesian or flooded
   conditions), measure the height of water above the TOC or use a
   staff gauge for ponded water.
6. Record date, time, depth to water, and any observations (e.g., well
   condition, nearby disturbance, wildlife activity) in the field
   notebook.
7. Replace and secure the well cap.

### Staff Gauge and Crest Gauge Reading

1. Read the water level on the staff gauge to the nearest 0.5 cm.
   Read at eye level to avoid parallax.
2. Record the reading, date, time, and any obstructions (debris on the
   gauge, algae).
3. For crest gauges: record the peak water mark left by granular cork
   or paint inside the gauge since the last visit. Reset the gauge
   per the manufacturer's instructions.

### Automated Logger Deployment and Download

1. Program the logger for the desired recording interval (typically
   15 minutes to 1 hour for wetland hydrology)
2. Deploy the logger in the well, suspended at a known depth below
   the TOC using a stainless steel cable or direct-read cable
3. Deploy a barometric logger above the expected high water line (for
   non-vented transducers)
4. Record the deployment details: logger serial number, deployment
   depth, start time, recording interval
5. On each visit, download data using the manufacturer's software.
   Take a manual water level measurement at the time of download for
   calibration verification.
6. Compensate pressure transducer data for barometric pressure changes
   using the barometric logger data. Most manufacturer software
   includes an automated compensation routine.

### Inundation Mapping

1. During each visit, note the spatial extent of surface water or
   saturated soil at the site
2. Record the inundation boundary on a site map or using GPS waypoints
3. Photograph fixed photo points to document seasonal changes in
   inundation
4. Record the presence of wetland hydrology indicators
   (oxidized rhizospheres, water-stained leaves, drift lines,
   sediment deposits, water marks on trees) per the Army Corps of
   Engineers wetland delineation manual [@usace1987]


## Quality Control

- Take a manual water level reading concurrent with every logger
  download to verify logger accuracy. If the manual reading and logger
  reading differ by more than 2 cm, troubleshoot the logger (drift,
  fouling, cable slip).
- Record duplicate manual readings at 10% of wells per visit (read,
  remove the tape, re-read). Duplicates should agree within 0.5 cm.
- Check e-line calibration against a measured standard (e.g., a
  surveyed depth) at least once per season.
- Maintain a well construction log with TOC elevations; re-survey
  TOC elevations annually or after ground disturbance (frost heave,
  animal activity, mowing).
- Archive raw logger files in the project data folder before any
  processing. Version-control all compensation and correction scripts
  per [SOP-L801](../lab_sops/SOP-L801-rstudio-github.qmd).


## Data Management

1. Enter manual water level data into the project database within
   48 hours of collection
2. Download, compensate, and archive logger data within 7 days of
   retrieval
3. Convert all water level data to a common datum (e.g., NAVD88 or a
   local benchmark) before analysis
4. Flag and document any data gaps, logger malfunctions, or well
   damage

## Training Record

Before performing wetland hydrology monitoring independently,
personnel must:

1. Read this SOP and [SOP-F001](SOP-F001-field-safety.qmd) in full
2. Observe a trained operator demonstrate manual water level
   measurement and logger download at an active monitoring site
3. Practice using the water level indicator (e-line) under supervision
   and demonstrate agreement within 0.5 cm on duplicate readings
4. Demonstrate competence in logger programming and data download
5. Be signed off by the PI or field lead
